catalog_quote: Contrary to Kodzasov’s (1999) claim, Northern Akhvakh is NOT a tone language. Northern Akhvakh is a typical word accent language in that, with the exception of morphologically complex words whose prosodic pattern may include secondary accents, the number of possible prosodic patterns for words with a given number of syllables never exceeds the number of syllables: there are two possible patterns for two-syllable word forms, three for three-syllable word forms, etc. What is however atypical is the realization of one of the possible patterns: in isolation, Northern Akhvakh word forms may show, either an accent on a non-final syllable, or no perceptible accentual contrast at all (which can therefore be analyzed as the realization of a word-final accent). Sec. 2.4 'Prosody' (the text layerdraft pp. 5-6) contains the quoted passage word for word: 'Contrary to Kodzasov's (1999) claim, Northern Akhvakh is NOT a tone language. Northern Akhvakh is a typical word accent language in that, with the exception of morphologically complex words whose prosodic pattern may include secondary accents, the number of possible prosodic patterns for words with a given number of syllables never exceeds the number of syllables: there are two possible patterns for two-syllable word form…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent, not tone; its position is not phonologically predictable: an n-syllable word has n possible patterns (accent on any non-final syllable, or 'accentless' = flat low contour, analysable as final accent), the choice being fixed by the lexicon and by morphological rules (Creissels 2010: e.g. disyllabic nouns are lexically either initial-accented or accentless; -Ca plural suffixes add an accent on the stem-final syllable, vowel-change plurals delete the lexical accent; stress alone distinguishes -wa perfective w-óq'-u-wa from potential w-oq'-ú-wa). Older first-hand sources characterise the same variety differently: Magomedbekova 1999: 254 'stress weak, dynamic, non-fixed'; Kodzasov (Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 323, same village Tad-Magitl') 'word stress absent, phrasal accent usually on the 1st syllable, syllabic tones H/L/R/F'. All three agree there is no fixed stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary accents only in morphologically complex words (sketch 2.4); Creissels 2010 pp. 5-6: when an accent-adding plural suffix attaches to a lexically accented noun both accents are retained (χ̄ṹk’ače -> χ̄ṹk’ačéla), with fluctuating relative prominence when adjacent (ráʁíla).
new_statements.exceptions: Accentless word class (no perceptible accent in isolation); context-conditioned final accent (e.g. es̄e vs es̄é 'our' depending on whether the following noun has initial accent, Creissels 2010 p. 4); a few nouns keep their accent in vowel-change plurals (ák’a -> ák’o 'woman', q̄’ačáʁa -> q̄’ačáʁo); Kodzasov's competing tonal analysis explicitly rejected as allophonic.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent as realised on word forms in isolation (citation forms); Creissels notes that syntactic / information-structure rules may add an accent on the last syllable of words in context, and Kodzasov 1990 speaks of phrasal accent on the 1st syllable. Variety: Northern Akhvakh, speakers from Tadmagitl' (and Lologonitl', Sovetskoe, Kamyškutan) = akhv1239 proper.
new_statements.identity_note: All three first-hand sources describe Northern Akhvakh proper (akhv1239): Creissels' data are from Tadmagitl', Lologonitl', Sovetskoe and Kamyškutan speakers (plus separate work on Axaxdərə Akhvakh in Azerbaijan, also Northern); Kodzasov's sketch is explicitly 's. Tad-Magitli'; Magomedbekova 1999 states her sketch uses Northern-dialect data. Southern Akhvakh (Cegob, Tljanub, Ratlub; sout3220-type varieties) is not covered by any of the statements.

sources.note: Sec. 2.4 Prosody (pp. 5-6): Northern Akhvakh is NOT a tone language (contra Kodzasov 1999) but a typical word-accent language: n possible prosodic patterns for n-syllable words; in isolation a word form shows either an accent on a non-final syllable or no perceptible accentual contrast (analysable as word-final accent); secondary accents only in morphologically complex words; rejects Kibrik & Kodzasov's seven disyllabic tone patterns (same village, Tadmagitl'). Fn. 11: stress distinguishes -wa perfective w-óq'-u-wa from potential w-oq'-ú-wa; fn. 28: 'here' vs 'where' distinguished by accentua…

sources.note: Whole paper on accent (corpus of ~3600 sentences, speaker I. Abdulaeva): contrast accented/unaccented syllables can be as sharp as in Russian or Spanish; accented words (accent on a non-final syllable) coexist with accentless words (flat, low contour); disyllabic nouns ó o or accentless, trisyllabic ó o o / o ó o / accentless (pp. 2-3); accent placement = lexical information + morphological rules (p. 4); plural suffixes -Ca add an accent on the stem-final syllable, vowel-change plurals delete the lexical accent, two accents may co-occur (pp. 5-6); syntactic/information-structure rules may add…

sources.note: p. 323, Slog i prosodija: '2. Словесное ударение отсутствует. Фразовый акцент помещается обычно на 1-й слог слова. 3. Система слоговых тонов стандартна: H, L, R, F.. В двусложных именах зафиксированы: HH, LL, HL, HF, RH, RL, RR' with minimal tonal pairs; p. 318: Akhvakh listed among languages whose tonal system was studied in detail with an accentuated wordlist; languages with syllabic tone usually lack word stress.
